title: Post-upgrade forensics and intermittent IO smoke probes
content:
Purpose:
This note is a lightweight investigative playbook for when clusters report intermittent install/runtime failures after a private deployment upgrade (VPC or on-prem). Focus is on IO/network flakiness, driver-related GPU hangs, and Terraform module drift that commonly surface as transient errors. Use this as the "first 30 minutes" triage script, plus a set of deterministic smoke probes to decide canary/rollback.

Scope and when to use:
- Post-upgrade (minor or major) when some nodes or pods report errors that do not immediately reproduce in a full cluster restart.
- Symptoms covered: pod CrashLoopBackOffs with IO errors, kubelet image pull timeouts, disk remount errors, unexpectedly high system call latency, NVMe/ephemeral disk timeouts, intermittent gRPC socket resets, and driver OOMs.
- Not intended for full SRE postmortem; this is to quickly gather signals and run short remediation steps.

High-level checklist (first 30 minutes):
1) Gather one-sentence symptom and scope: "what fails", "how many nodes/pods", "first-seen timestamp".
2) Check upgrade change list: which terraform modules, driver versions, and kernel packages changed.
3) Run global smoke probes (below) against a sample of 3 node types (control plane, GPU worker, storage-heavy worker).
4) If smoke probes show systemic failure, preserve nodes (no reboot) and start live forensic capture (sar, iostat, tcpdump, dmesg).
5) If failures are isolated to canary subset, consider rollback for that canary and continue investigating remaining nodes.

Quick smoke probes (runnable over SSH, expect <5m each):
- Kube API sanity: kubectl get nodes -o wide; kubectl get pods -A | grep -iE "CrashLoopBackOff|ImagePullBackOff|ErrImagePull"
- Node health: ssh node 'systemctl is-failed kubelet etcd docker || echo OK; uptime; free -h'
- Disk IO basic: ssh node 'sudo dmesg | tail -n50 | grep -iE "nvme|scsi|I/O|timeout|blk"'
- Small IO stress: ssh node 'sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/io-test bs=1M count=256 oflag=direct conv=fsync && echo SUCCESS || echo FAIL'
- NFS/CIFS mounts: ssh node 'mount | grep -E "nfs|cifs"; sudo stat -c "%n %F %s" /var/lib/redwood || true'
- Network RTTs: ssh node 'ping -c 5 8.8.8.8; ip route show | head -n1'
- GPU quick-check (GPU workers): ssh node 'nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,driver_version --format=csv' or for AMD ROCm check dmesg for amdgpu errors
- Kubelet log tail: ssh node 'sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager | tail -n50'

Forensic commands and what to look for:
Network:
- sudo tcpdump -n -i any port 7070 or port 50051 -c 200 -w /tmp/trace.pcap (look for retransmits, RSTs, or sudden bursts)
- ss -tuna | grep ESTAB (look for too many connections to model servers)
Storage/IO:
- sudo iostat -x 1 5 (look for %util ~100 and svctm high)
- sudo fio --filename=/tmp/fio-test --direct=1 --rw=randread --bs=4k --size=256M --numjobs=4 --time_based --runtime=30s --group_reporting (timeouts or large lat spikes indicate underlying device issues)
- cat /proc/mdstat; lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,RO,TYPE,MOUNTPOINT
System/kernel:
- sudo dmesg | grep -i -E "oom|hung_task|lockup|GPU|nvidia|amdgpu|nvme|blk"
- journalctl -k -n 500 --no-pager | tail -n200
Kube/k8s runtime:
- kubectl describe pod <bad-pod> -n <ns> (look for events: Back-off restarting failed container; Failed to create pod sandbox: network plugin not ready)
- kubectl logs <pod> --previous --tail=200
Terraform/module checks (quick):
- Check applied module versions: cat terraform.lock.hcl and the module registry blocks in modules/
- terraform state list | grep <module_name> (verify resources present)
- terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -out=/tmp/plan.tfplan (on a replica workspace) to catch drift; exit code 2 indicates changes
- If workspace uses remote state, confirm state lock/unlock history in backend (S3/DynamoDB, GCS)

Concrete hypothesis mapping (indicator => likely cause => quick remediation):
- Repeated NVMe timeouts in dmesg => underlying ephemeral disk firmware bug or overloaded host IO => evict pods from host, mark node unschedulable, replace host, or apply vendor firmware patch.
- Kubelet image pullbacks with intermittent 404/timeout => transient registry auth issue or MTU mismatch on VPC overlay => test curl to registry from node and check if jumbo frames/MTU differ between nodes.
- GPU driver errors (nvidia-smi failing intermittently) => mismatched driver/toolkit/kernel versions from upgrade => verify driver packages installed, compare /var/log/nvidia-installer.log and kernel module version (modinfo nvidia). If mismatch, pin driver version or roll back nodes.
- TLS handshake resets between model-router and runtime => wrong CA bundle in agent config or rotated certs not deployed => check cert expiry (openssl s_client -connect) and agent logs for x509 errors.
- Terraform apply changed security group or route table causing asymmetric routing => confirm VPC route tables and ephemeral ENI attachments, revert change for the subset if needed.

Mini playbook: when to pause rollout vs roll forward
- Pause rollout (rollback canary) if: >20% of production nodes show IO or kernel errors; persistent dmesg nvme/scsi errors; or terraform plan shows unintentional state drift.
- Continue rollout if: failures limited to single AZ with known maintenance window; smoke-tests pass on >90% of nodes; observed issues limited to non-critical test workloads.

Example evidence capture commands to attach to ticket (one-liners):
- kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Failed -o wide > /tmp/failed-pods.txt
- for n in $(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do echo "=== $n ==="; ssh $n "uname -a; sudo dmesg | tail -n50; sudo iostat -x 1 3"; done > /tmp/nodes-quick-forensics.txt

Terraform module notes (common pitfalls we see):
- Modules with wildcard provider versions allow provider upgrades during apply; pin provider version in root module.
- Remote state drift when state file hasn't been updated after manual changes (ops sometimes touch route tables). Always run terraform import on any manual resource you intend to keep.
- Be careful with null_resource triggers that run local-exec during apply; they can reconfigure nodes unexpectedly during upgrades. Prefer a separate orchestration step if possible.

Upgrade safety gates (pre-flight checks):
- Automatic: terraform plan shows zero changes for infra modules; container images exist in registry and are pullable from a test node; drivers and kernel packages listed in the upgrade manifest are available in apt/yum repo.
- Manual: run smoke-tests on a canary VPC/subnet and note pass rate >95% for IO and network probes.
- Canary rollback triggers: >3 nodes with GPU driver failures OR any node with repeated kernel OOM/hung_task OR >5% increase in 5xxs to model endpoints for 15m.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Capture a small pcap example that shows a model client RST during a large response (Samira to reproduce on staging).
- Add automated fio-based IO smoke test to preflight pipeline (idea: run 30s randread on ephemeral).
- Consider adding a terraform static analyzer job in CI to detect security-group route changes.

Escalation matrix:
- Eng oncall (primary): paged via PagerDuty (driver/kernel/hung task)
- Infra lead (Marco) for terraform/state issues
- Applied ML (Aisha) for model-serving performance regressions

Unresolved questions:
- At what node count threshold do we auto-abort canary? (current heuristic: 3+ nodes in different racks)
- How long to wait between reboots of a node suspected of transient NVMe firmware hiccup? (30m recommended, but sometimes vendor suggests immediate replacement)

If you run this and collect artifacts, paste traces into JIRA INF-4827 with tags: "post-upgrade-forensics" and add @eng-private-deployments for visibility.

End.
